title: Kitchen and Summer
premise: Gideon Villalobos, a once-celebrated cellist whose hands froze mid-concert, retreats to her late grandmother's crumbling orchard intending to sell it and disappear. But the deed inexplicably names a second heir: Marisol Ferreira, the childhood friend she betrayed and hasn't spoken to in fifteen years, who arrives with festival plans, a repair crew of misfits, and no intention of leaving. As the two women are forced into an uneasy partnership restoring the orchard in time for its centennial harvest festival, Gideon confronts how her family's inherited wealth and control poisoned every relationship she had—including with herself. When a developer backed by Gideon's estranged father moves to seize the land, she must perform again, publicly and imperfectly, choosing the found family she built over the legacy that broke her; the novel ends with the festival saved, forgiveness offered but honestly incomplete, and Gideon playing not flawlessly, but freely.
about_author: Sable Whitlock is the pen name of a former orchard worker turned novelist who writes about inheritance, music, and the families we choose. She lives near a failing apple farm she refuses to let anyone fix.

chapters.title: The Deed That Wouldn't Die
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Three months after her catastrophic final performance, Gideon arrives at her grandmother's orchard with a realtor's number and a plan to sell fast. The county clerk reveals the deed names two heirs: her and Marisol Ferreira. Emotional beat: dread disguised as efficiency—the past arriving before she's ready.

chapters.title: Marisol, Uninvited
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol arrives with a borrowed truck, three volunteers, and fifteen years of silence behind her. She claims her half of the deed and refuses Gideon's buyout offer on the spot. Emotional beat: defiant warmth meeting frozen hostility; the reader sees Marisol's hurt beneath her armor.

chapters.title: Rules of Coexistence
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Forced into a temporary truce, they draft absurdly specific cohabitation rules while surveying the decaying orchard—and discover a developer's letter offering Gideon's father money for the land. Emotional beat: grudging comedy curdling into unease as old power enters the picture.

chapters.title: What Grandmother Kept
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Cleaning the farmhouse, they find letters revealing their grandmother secretly kept both girls connected for years—paying Marisol's tuition anonymously after Gideon's betrayal. Emotional beat: grief and guilt; Gideon realizes her grandmother was engineering this reunion all along.

chapters.title: The Festival Committee
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The town's centennial harvest festival needs the orchard as its venue, and Marisol commits them—volunteering Gideon without asking. A ragtag committee of locals becomes an accidental found family. Emotional beat: reluctant belonging; Gideon watches herself being pulled into community despite her protests.

chapters.title: Strings, Retuned
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. A broken cello surfaces in the barn—her grandmother's—and a committee kid begs Gideon to teach her. Gideon's hands shake through the first lesson, but she doesn't stop. Emotional beat: fragile hope; music returning as gift rather than performance.

chapters.title: The Father's Offer
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Her father arrives with lawyers and a check, revealing he engineered the dual deed to force the sale—and that he's been watching her failure with satisfaction. Marisol overhears him call Gideon worthless. Emotional beat: humiliation weaponized; the theme of inherited corruption made explicit.

chapters.title: Fifteen Years, Spoken
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The betrayal finally aired: what Gideon did at sixteen, why Marisol left, and how each has rewritten the story since. It ends worse than it starts—Marisol packs her truck. Emotional beat: devastating honesty; the midpoint rupture where truth costs more than silence.

chapters.title: The Night Before the Festival
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. With Marisol gone and the developer filing an emergency claim, the committee refuses to cancel. Gideon discovers her father forged part of the paperwork and decides to fight—not with lawyers, but by taking the festival stage. Emotional beat: resolve; the invisible woman choosing visibility.

chapters.title: Harvest
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. At the festival, Gideon plays the cello publicly for the first time since her collapse—imperfect, trembling, alive—while exposing the forged documents. Marisol returns mid-song. Forgiveness is offered, accepted slowly, not fully earned yet. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution; second chances taken with bad timing anyway.
